- If sentiment is positive (≥0.25) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.00) or flat, model often overcorrects downward; allow slight upward bias to avoid premature bottoming.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct; apply a “cool-down” decay to forecast slope.
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 90), model often fails to recognize it; adjust forecast to align with recent low trend.
- If history shows volatility clustering (e.g., 3+ consecutive price drops), model tends to underestimate further drops; add a downward bias buffer.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often overestimates early in the horizon (first 5–7 days); apply a “lag correction” by reducing first 5 days’ forecast by 1–2% relative to history.
- If sentiment history includes multiple 0.25–0.50 values, model tends to overreact to sentiment; dampen forecast sensitivity to sentiment spikes.
